On β=6\beta=6 Tracy-Widom distribution and the second Calogero-Painlevé system

Alexander Its A. R. ItsDepartment of Mathematical Sciences, Indiana University, Indianapolis, 402 N. Blackford St. Indianapolis, IN 46202, USA, & St. Petersburg State University, 7/9 Universitetskaya nab. 199034 St. Petersburg, Russia. Email address: aits@iu.edu and Andrei Prokhorov A. O. ProkhorovDepartment of Mathematical Sciences, University of Cincinnati, 2600 Clifton Ave, Cincinnati, OH, 45221, USA & St. Petersburg State University, 7/9 Universitetskaya nab. 199034 St. Petersburg, Russia Email address: prokhoai@umail.uc.edu
Abstract.

The Calogero-Painlevé systems were introduced in 2001 by K. Takasaki as a natural generalization of the classical Painlevé equations to the case of the several Painlevé “particles” coupled via the Calogero type interactions. In 2014, I. Rumanov discovered the remarkable fact that a particular case of the second Calogero-Painlevé II equation describes the Tracy-Widom distribution function for the general beta-ensembles with even values of the parameter beta. Most recently, in 2017 work of M. Bertola, M. Cafasso, and V. Rubtsov, it was proven that all Calogero-Painlevé systems are Lax integrable, and hence their solutions admit a Riemann-Hilbert representation. This important observation has opened the door to rigorous, based on the Deift-Zhou nonlinear steepest descent method, asymptotic analysis of the Calogero-Painlevé equations. This in turn yields the possibility of rigorous evaluation of the asymptotic behavior of the Tracy-Widom distributions for the values of beta beyond the classical β=1,2,4.\beta=1,2,4. In this work we shall start an asymptotic analysis of the Calogero-Painlevé system with a special focus on the Calogero-Painlevé system corresponding to β=6\beta=6 Tracy-Widom distribution function. The principle technical challenge is the implementation of the nonlinear steepest descent approach beyond the 2×22\times 2 matrix dimension of the corresponding Riemann-Hilbert problem; in our case, it is 6×66\times 6.

Key words and phrases: 
asymptotic analysis, Riemann-Hilbert problems, beta ensembles, Tracy-Widom distribution, Calogero-Painlevé systems.

1. Introduction and Main Result

1.1. Calogero-Painlevé system

Denote xj​(t)x_{j}(t), j=1,…,nj=1,...,n the positions of nn 1D particles. The second Calogero-Painlevé model is the dynamical system given by the equations

(1.1) xk′′=2xk3+txk+θ+2g2∑j≠k1(xk−xj)3,k=1,…nx_{k}^{\prime\prime}=2x_{k}^{3}+tx_{k}+\theta+2g^{2}\sum_{j\neq k}\frac{1}{(x_{k}-x_{j})^{3}},\quad k=1,...n

These are Hamiltonian equations,

xk′=∂H∂yk=yk,xk′′=yk′=−∂H∂xk,x^{\prime}_{k}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial y_{k}}=y_{k},\quad x^{\prime\prime}_{k}=y^{\prime}_{k}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial x_{k}},

with the Hamiltonian,

(1.2) H=∑k=1n(yk22−xk42−xk2​t2−θ​xk)+g2​∑j<k1(xk−xj)2.H=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_{k}^{2}}{2}-\frac{x_{k}^{4}}{2}-\frac{x_{k}^{2}t}{2}-\theta x_{k}\right)+g^{2}\sum_{j<k}\frac{1}{(x_{k}-x_{j})^{2}}.

System (1.1) can be thought of as a collection of the n independent Painlevé II particles interacting via the classical Calogero potential. This system was introduced by K. Takasaki in 2001 [22], together with five other similar systems associated with each of the remaining five Painlevé equations, as non-autonomous generalization of the Inozemtsev systems [16]. The Calogero-Painlevé VI version of the model had also showed up in a completely different context in the work of P. Etingof, W. L. Gan, and A. Oblomkov [11] in connection with their study of the generalized double affine algebras of higher rank. Our principal interest in system (1.1) is its relation, discovered by I. Rumanov [20, 21, 19], to the Tracy-Widom distribution function of the general beta-ensemble of random matrices.

1.2. General beta-ensemble and Calogero-Painlevé systems .

Given β>0\beta>0, Dyson’s β\beta-ensemble is defined as a Coulomb gas of NN charged particles, that is as the space of NN one dimensional particles, {−∞<λ1<λ2<…<λN<∞}\{-\infty<\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}<...<\lambda_{N}<\infty\} with the probability density given by the equation,

(1.3) p(λ1,…,λN)dλ1…dλN=1ZN∏1≤j,k≤N|λj−λk|βe−β∑j=1NV(λj)dλ1…dλN.p(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{N})\mathrm{d}\lambda_{1}\ldots\mathrm{d}\lambda_{N}=\frac{1}{Z_{N}}\prod_{1\leq j,k\leq N}|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k}|^{\beta}{\rm e}^{-\beta\sum_{j=1}^{N}V(\lambda_{j})}\mathrm{d}\lambda_{1}\ldots\mathrm{d}\lambda_{N}.
(1.4) ZN=∫−∞∞…∫−∞∞∏1≤j,k≤N|λj−λk|βe−β∑j=1NV(λj)dλ1…dλNZ_{N}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}...\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\prod_{1\leq j,k\leq N}|\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k}|^{\beta}{\rm e}^{-\beta\sum_{j=1}^{N}V(\lambda_{j})}\mathrm{d}\lambda_{1}\ldots\mathrm{d}\lambda_{N}

Here, V⁡(λ)V(\lambda) has a meaning of external field which we will assume to be Gaussian, i.e. V⁡(λ)=λ22V(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}. The objects of interest are the gap probabilities in the large NN limit. We will be particularly concerned with the soft edge probability distribution

(1.5) Fβ​(t)≡Eβsoft​(0,(t,∞))=limN→∞Eβ​Nsoft​(0,(2​N+t2​N1/6,∞)),F_{\beta}(t)\equiv E_{\beta}^{\mbox{soft}}\Bigl(0;(t,\infty)\Bigr)=\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}E_{\beta N}^{\mbox{soft}}\left(0;\Bigl(\sqrt{2N}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{2}N^{1/6}},\infty\Bigr)\right),

where

(1.6) Eβ​Nsoft​(0,(t,∞))=∫−∞t…​∫−∞tp⁡(λ1,…,λN)​d​λ1​…​d​λN.E_{\beta N}^{\mbox{soft}}\Bigl(0;(t,\infty)\Bigr)=\int_{-\infty}^{t}...\int_{-\infty}^{t}p(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{N})\mathrm{d}\lambda_{1}\ldots\mathrm{d}\lambda_{N}.

It was shown in [7] that this distribution is the same for a large class of potentials V⁡(λ)V(\lambda). Cases β=1,2,4\beta=1,2,4 known as Gaussian orthogonal (GOE), Gaussian unitary (GUE) and Gaussian symplectic (GSE) ensembles. In fact, in these cases, the distribution (1.3) describes the statistics of the eigenvalues of orthogonal, Hermitian, and symplectic random matrices, respectively, with i.i.d. matrix entries. The corresponding limiting edge distribution functions Fβ​(s)F_{\beta}(s) are then becoming the classical Tracy-Widom distributions [23, 24]. They admit explicit representations either as the Airy kernel Fredholm determinants or in terms of the Hastings-McLeod solution of the second Painlevé equation. These representations, in turn, allow one to evaluate the asymptotic expansions of Fβ​(t)F_{\beta}(t) as t→±∞t\to\pm\infty, i.e. the so-called tail asymptotics.

A principal issue is the asymptotic analysis of Fβ​(s)F_{\beta}(s) beyond the classical values β=1,2,4\beta=1,2,4. The crux of the problem is that the orthogonal polynomial approach, which is the principal technique in the random matrix case, is not available for general β\beta. However, several highly nontrivial conjectures concerning the general β\beta ensembles have been suggested. An excellent presentation of the state of the art in this area is given in the survey by P. Forrester [13]. The current principal heuristic result concerning the asymptotic behavior of the generalized Tracy-Widom distribution Fβ​(t)F_{\beta}(t) was obtained in 2010 by G. Borot, B. Eynard, S. N. Majumdar and C. Nadal and it reads as follows.

Conjecture 1.1 ([5]).
(1.7) Fβ​(t)=\displaystyle F_{\beta}(t)= exp⁡(−β​|t|324+23​(β/2−1)​|t|3/2CLOSE\displaystyle\exp\left(-\beta\frac{|t|^{3}}{24}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\Bigl(\beta/2-1\Bigr)|t|^{3/2}\right.

The constant term χ\chi is also explicitly predicted. Indeed, it is claimed that

(1.9) χ=\displaystyle\chi= β2​(112−ζ′​(−1))+γ6​β−log⁡2​π4−log⁡(β/2)2\displaystyle\frac{\beta}{2}\left(\frac{1}{12}-\zeta^{\prime}(-1)\right)+\frac{\gamma}{6\beta}-\frac{\log 2\pi}{4}-\frac{\log(\beta/2)}{2}

Formulae (1.7) – (1.11) have been derived in [5, 6] within the framework of the so-called loop-equation technique by performing the relevant double scaling limit directly in the formal large NN expansion of the multiple integral in (1.6).

Remark 1.3.

For even β\beta the integral above was evaluated in [5] as

∫0∞1eβ​t/2−1(tet−1−1+t2−t212)d​tt2=−∑m=1β/2−12​mβlogΓ(2​mβ)+2βζ′(−1)−log⁡(β/2)6​β\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{\beta t/2}-1}\left(\frac{t}{\mathrm{e}^{t}-1}-1+\frac{t}{2}-\frac{t^{2}}{12}\right)\frac{\mathrm{d}t}{t^{2}}=-\sum_{m=1}^{\beta/2-1}\frac{2m}{\beta}\log\Gamma\left(\frac{2m}{\beta}\right)+\frac{2}{\beta}\zeta^{\prime}(-1)-\frac{\log(\beta/2)}{6\beta}

Remark 1.4.

Rigorous derivation of (1.7) – (1.9), for the basic classical case β=2\beta=2 is given by P. Deift et al in [8] and in [1]. In [1] the cases β=1,4\beta=1,4 are also done. Both papers use the Riemann-Hilbert method which is available to the classical cases of β=1,2,4\beta=1,2,4. The formula (1.11) for that cases was known already in [23, 24].

Remark 1.5.

The leading asymptotic term in (1.7) for arbitrary β\beta has been rigorously obtained in [18] with the help of the analysis of the certain stochastic Schrödinger operator.

(1.12) Fβ​(t)=\displaystyle F_{\beta}(t)= exp⁡(−β​|t|324​(1+o⁡(1))),t→−∞.\displaystyle\exp\left(-\beta\frac{|t|^{3}}{24}(1+o(1))\right),\quad t\to-\infty.

We shall mention this paper again in the next paragraph. Similarly the right tail estimate for arbitrary β\beta was obtained in [9]

(1.13) Fβ(t)=1−t−3​β4+o[(logt)−1/2]e−2​β3​t3/2,t→∞.\displaystyle F_{\beta}(t)=1-t^{-\frac{3\beta}{4}+o[(\log t)^{-1/2}]}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{2\beta}{3}t^{3/2}},\quad t\rightarrow\infty.
Remark 1.6.

Similarly to continuous ensemble (1.3), the discrete β\beta ensemble was introduced in [4]. The largest particle behavior is described by the same Tracy-Widom β\beta distribution. The corresponding universality was shown in [15].

It is remarkable, that paper [5], while giving a such detailed formulae for the asymptotics of the dustribution function Fβ​(t)F_{\beta}(t) does not actually produce any description of the object itself (for the finite values of tt). The latter has been done by A. Bloemendal and B. Virag [3]. Inspired by the pioneering work of E. Dumitriu and A. Edelman [10] and by subsequent works [26] and [18], Bloemendal and Virag [3] have connected the analysis of the generalized Tracy-Widom distribution Fβ​(t)F_{\beta}(t) with the study of stochastic Schrödinger operators. In particular, it has been proven in [3] that the Tracy-Widom distribution function Fβ​(t)F_{\beta}(t), for any β\beta, can be expressed in terms of the solution of a certain linear PDE. In more detail, the result of [3] can be formulated as follows.

Consider the partial differential equation,

(1.14) ∂F∂t+2β​∂2F∂x2+(t−x2)​∂F∂x=0,(x,t)∈ℝ2\frac{\partial F}{\partial t}+\frac{2}{\beta}\frac{\partial^{2}F}{\partial x^{2}}+(t-x^{2})\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=0,\quad(x,t)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2}

supplemented by the boundary conditions,

(1.15) F⁡(x,t)→1,asx,t→∞,togetherF(x,t)\to 1,\quad\mbox{as}\quad x,t\to\infty,\quad\mbox{together}

and

(1.16) F⁡(x,t)→0,asx→−∞,for fixed t.F(x,t)\to 0,\quad\mbox{as}\quad x\to-\infty,\quad\mbox{for fixed $t$.}
Theorem 1.7 ([3]).

The boundary value problem (1.14), (1.15), (1.16) has a unique bounded smooth solution. Moreover, equation,

(1.17) Fβ​(t)=limx→∞F⁡(x,t),F_{\beta}(t)=\lim_{x\to\infty}F(x,t),

determines the Tracy-Widom distribution function for the general value of the parameter β>0\beta>0.

The boundary value problem (1.14) – (1.16) is an efficient tool for numerical evaluation of Tracy-Widom distribution, see [25]. The next step in the studying of Fβ​(t)F_{\beta}(t) has been done in the works of I. Rumanov, [20, 21, 19], who, in the case of even values of the parameter β\beta, has reduced the analysis of the Bloemendal-Virag equation to the analysis of an auxiliary system of nonlinear ODEs. For the first nontrivial case, β=6\beta=6, Rumanov has obtained the following representation for F6​(t)F_{6}(t),

logF6(3−2/3t)=13∫t∞(u4(s)+su2(s)−(u′(s))2)ds\log F_{6}(3^{-2/3}t)=\frac{1}{3}\int_{t}^{\infty}\Bigl(u^{4}(s)+su^{2}(s)-(u^{\prime}(s))^{2}\Bigr)\mathrm{d}s
(1.18) +23∫t∞α(s)ds−13∫t∞u′u(s)(1+γ(s))ds+log(1−γ⁡(t)2).+\frac{2}{3}\int_{t}^{\infty}\alpha(s)\mathrm{d}s-\frac{1}{3}\int_{t}^{\infty}\frac{u^{\prime}}{u}(s)\Bigl(1+\gamma(s)\Bigr)\mathrm{d}s+\log\left(\frac{1-\gamma(t)}{2}\right).

Here, the function u⁡(t)u(t) is the Hastings-McLeod second Painlevé transcendent, i.e. the solution of the second Painlevé equation,

(1.19) u′′=t​u+2​u3,u^{\prime\prime}=tu+2u^{3},

uniquely determined by the condition,

(1.20) u∼12​π​t14​e−23​t32,t→+∞,u\sim\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\pi}t^{\frac{1}{4}}}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{2}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}}},\quad t\rightarrow+\infty,

while the pair of the functions (γ⁡(t),α⁡(t))(\gamma(t),\alpha(t)) is defined as the solution of the system of the first order ODEs,

(1.21) γ′=23​α​γ+u′u​(1+γ)​(2−γ)3,α′=α⁡(23​α+u′u​2−γ3)−t6​(1+γ)−u23​(3+γ).\gamma^{\prime}=\frac{2}{3}\alpha\gamma+\frac{u^{\prime}}{u}\frac{(1+\gamma)(2-\gamma)}{3},\quad\alpha^{\prime}=\alpha\left(\frac{2}{3}\alpha+\frac{u^{\prime}}{u}\frac{2-\gamma}{3}\right)-\frac{t}{6}(1+\gamma)-\frac{u^{2}}{3}(3+\gamma).

with the asymptotic conditions,

(1.22) γ∼−1+18​π​t32​e−43​t32,α∼316​π​t​e−43​t32,t→∞\gamma\sim-1+\frac{1}{8\pi t^{\frac{3}{2}}}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{4}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}}},\quad\alpha\sim\frac{3}{16\pi t}\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{4}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}}},\quad t\rightarrow\infty

It should be mentioned that Rumanov’s derivation of the above results is based on certain heuristic assumptions which have been highlighted and some of them proven in [14]. However, the proof of a key assumption that the asymptotic conditions (1.22) determine a unique smooth solution of system (1.21), has not been yet found11 1 Although, there are very strong numerical evidence produced by YuQi Li from East China Normal University that this statement is true (see [17])..

In more details, the relation of Rumanov’s equations (1.21), (1.22) and the Bloemendal -Virág boundary value problem (1.14) – (1.16) can be described as follows (here we follow the interpretation of Rumanov’s results given in [14]).

Let u⁡(t)u(t) γ⁡(t)\gamma(t), α⁡(t)\alpha(t) be the objects defined in (1.19) – (1.22). Also let Ψ0​(x,t)\Psi_{0}(x,t) be the fundamental solution of the first equation of Painlevé II Lax pair

(1.23) d​Ψ0d​x=L​Ψ0,L=x22​σ3+x​(0uu0)+(−t2−u2−u′u′t2+u2)\displaystyle\dfrac{d\Psi_{0}}{dx}={L}\Psi_{0},\qquad{L}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}\sigma_{3}+x\begin{pmatrix}0&u\\ u&0\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}-\dfrac{t}{2}-u^{2}&-u^{\prime}\\ u^{\prime}&\dfrac{t}{2}+u^{2}\end{pmatrix}

and

Then (see [14]) the solution of boundary value problem (1.14), (1.15), (1.16) for β=6\beta=6 is given by

(1.27) F(3−1/3x,3−2/3t)=κex36−x​t2[u−12(1+γ2x−α)Ψ0,12(x,t)+u12Ψ0,22(x,t)].\displaystyle F\big(3^{-1/3}x,3^{-2/3}t\big)=\kappa\mathrm{e}^{\frac{x^{3}}{6}-\frac{xt}{2}}\left[u^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left(\frac{1+\gamma}{2}x-\alpha\right)\Psi_{0,12}(x,t)+u^{\frac{1}{2}}\Psi_{0,22}(x,t)\right].

We are now going to explain the appearance in the picture of the Calogero-Painlevé system. To this end, let us pass from the triple of the functions (u⁡(t),γ⁡(t),α⁡(t))(u(t),\gamma(t),\alpha(t)) to the triple (Q1​(t),Q2​(t),Q3​(t))(Q_{1}(t),Q_{2}(t),Q_{3}(t)), according to the equations,

e1=−4​α​γ1−γ2−u′u​1+γ1−γ,e2=41−γ2​[−α2+u2−(1+γ)​(t2+u2+α​u′u)],e_{1}=-\frac{4\alpha\gamma}{1-\gamma^{2}}-\frac{u^{\prime}}{u}\frac{1+\gamma}{1-\gamma},\quad e_{2}=\frac{4}{1-\gamma^{2}}\left[-\alpha^{2}+u^{2}-(1+\gamma)\left(\frac{t}{2}+u^{2}+\alpha\frac{u^{\prime}}{u}\right)\right],

Therefore, we arrive at the following connection problem for the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29):

Show that there is a unique solution, (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)), of (1.29) which is smooth for all real tt and which behaves at t=−∞t=-\infty and t=∞t=\infty as it is indicated in equations (1.36) and (1.40), respectively, up to permutation.

In this paper we address this problem using the Riemann-Hilbert representation of the solutions of the Calogero-Painlevé system which was found in the recent work [2] and which we will now describe in some details.

1.4. The Riemann-Hilbert representation of the Calogero-Painlevé particles.

In [2], it is shown (in fact, for the general case of nn particles) that the system (1.29) is Lax-pair integrable, and the following Riemann-Hilbert representation of its general solution takes place.

Riemann-Hilbert problem 1.8.

The first principal question now is which Riemann-Hilbert data, i.e. the matrices AA, BB and CC, yield the solution of the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29) that corresponds to the Tracy-Widom function F6​(t)F_{6}(t). The main result of this paper is the following partial answer to this question.

Theorem 1.9.

Consider the Riemann-Hilbert problem 1.8 with matrices A,B,C,EA,B,C,E satisfying cyclic condition (1.47).

  1. (1)

    The solution Ψ⁡(z)≡Ψ⁡(z,t)\Psi(z)\equiv\Psi(z,t) and the corresponding 3×33\times 3 matrix q0​(t)q_{0}(t) from (1.48) exist as meromorphic functions of tt.

  2. (2)

    Assume that matrices A,B,CA,B,C are parametrized by b11,b22,b21,b31b_{11},b_{22},b_{21},b_{31} and a33∈{i,e−5​π​i6}a_{33}\in\{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{5\pi\mathrm{i}}{6}}\} using formulas (3.3), (3.5) with b12=b23=1b_{12}=b_{23}=1. Then the eigenvalues (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))\Bigl(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)\Bigr)

    of the matrix q0​(t)q_{0}(t) form a family of solutions of the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29) whose behavior as t→−∞t\to-\infty is given by the asymptotic formulae (1.36) up to permutation.

  3. (3)

    Assume that matrices A,B,CA,B,C are parametrized by a11,a12,a13,b13a_{11},a_{12},a_{13},b_{13} using formulas (3.2), (3.4) with b12=b23=1b_{12}=b_{23}=1. Then the eigenvalues (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))\Bigl(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)\Bigr) of the matrix q0​(t)q_{0}(t) form the solutions of the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29) whose behavior as t→∞t\to\infty is given by the asymptotic formulae (1.40) up to permutation.

The proof of this theorem is based on the Deift-Zhou nonlinear steepest descent method. As it has already been indicated in the Abstract, the principle technical challenge is the high matrix size of the associated Riemann-Hilbert problem, i.e., Riemann-Hilbert problem 1.8. Indeed, the higher than 2 matrix dimension leads to a considerable complications in two basic steps of the Deift-Zhou method, i.e. the contour deformation and the analysis of the local parametrices. We want to highlight specifically the difficulties related to the local parametrices. Indeed, in 2×22\times 2 case and in generic situation the modal Riemann-Hilbert problems corresponding to local parametrices always admit explicit solutions in classical special functions. Beyond the 2×22\times 2 matrix setting this is generally not the case any more. However, the specifics of the Riemann-Hilbert problem 1.8 has allowed us to solve all the relevant local model Riemann-Hilbert problems explicitly, in terms of the parabolic cylinder, Bessel, Airy, and confluent hypergeometric functions.

By considering the choice (3.6) of the RH data corresponding to intersection of parametrization (3.2), (3.4) and (3.3), (3.5) we arrive at the following corollary which is our key result.

Corollary 1.10.

The choice (3.6) of the RH data generates the solution of the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29) with both, the asymptotics (1.36) as t→−∞t\to-\infty and the asymptotics (1.40) as t→∞t\to\infty.

The still open questions are:

  • •

    To show that the choice (3.6) corresponding to intersection of parametrizations (3.2), (3.4) and (3.3), (3.5) guarantees that the Riemann-Hilbert problem is solvable for all real tt and that the corresponding solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) of the Calogero-Painlevé system exists and is smooth for all real tt.

  • •

    To show that the choice (3.6) yields the solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) which indeed generates the Tracy-Widom distribution F6​(t)F_{6}(t) and hence to prove the BEMN conjecture (1.9) for β=6\beta=6 (without the constant term χ\chi). The first issue here is to show that the above determined solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) is the unique solution of (1.29) that satisfies simultaneously the asymptotic conditions (1.36) and (1.40). It should be noticed that the asymptotics (1.36) by itself do not define the solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) uniquely–there is an “unseen” exponentially small term in it, and hence it can not be easily transformed back to the asymptotics (1.22) for the functions γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) and α⁡(t)\alpha(t). Presumably, the second asymptotics, i.e. formula (1.40), fixes the solution uniquely. The second issue is to show that the Bloemendal-Virag function F⁡(x,t)F(x,t) defined by the solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) via (1.27) (and automatically satisfying (1.14)) is bounded, smooth and satisfies the boundary conditions (1.15), (1.16).

  • •

    To evaluate rigorously χ\chi.

  • •

    To extend the result to arbitrary even β\beta.

There is one more open question which we want to emphasize. As we already mentioned before, asymptotics (1.40) of the solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) of the Calogero-Painlevé system yield (without the constant χ\chi) the BEMN asymptotics (1.37) for the Tracy-Widom function F6​(t)F_{6}(t) as t→−∞t\to-\infty. At the same time, asymptotics (1.36) does not reproduce BN asymptotics (1.31) of F6​(t)F_{6}(t) as t→∞t\to\infty . Indeed, direct substitution of (1.36) into (1.30) only produces the estimate,

(1.49) F6​(t)=1+O⁡(1tp),t→∞,\displaystyle F_{6}(t)=1+O\left(\frac{1}{t^{p}}\right),\quad t\to\infty,

with p=232p=\frac{23}{2}. Moreover, if we calculate more terms in the asymptotic formulae (1.36) , the value of the exponent pp will increase. In fact, one can conjecture that substitution of our Calogero-Painlevé solution into (1.30) would lead to the exponential type estimate,

(1.50) F6​(t)=1+O⁡(1t∞),t→∞.F_{6}(t)=1+O\left(\frac{1}{t^{\infty}}\right),\quad t\to\infty.

The question is how to make it as precise as in (1.31). In Appendix F we show how the similar problem can be resolved in the case of β=2\beta=2. Also, in this Appendix, following the β=2\beta=2 experience we shall outline a strategy how we think the right tail problem can be resolved. We intend to address all these questions in the forthcoming publication. We also want to point out that the reconstruction of the asymptotics (1.11) from the asymptotics (1.40) of the solution (x1​(t),x2​(t),x3​(t))(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),x_{3}(t)) is equivalent to reconstruction of the asymptotics (1.22) of the functions γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) and α⁡(t)\alpha(t) and, in fact, is closely related to the resolution of the issues indicated in the second open question above.

1.5. Plan of the paper

In the next Section 2, we shall present, following [2], the isomonodromy Lax pair for the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29). Then, in the beginning of Section 3, following again [2], we will transform the Lax formalism for the Calogero-Painlevé system to its Riemann-Hilbert formalism. The main body of the paper consists of Subsections 4 and 5 where we perform an asymptotic analysis of the Bertola-Cafasso-Rubtsov Riemann-Hilbert problem as t→∞t\to\infty and t→−∞t\to-\infty, respectively. The specific structure of the jump matrices announced in Theorem 1.9 will be fixed in a process of application of the Deift-Zhou nonlinear steepest descent method which will eventually lead us to the proof of the Theorem. In fact, and we will say more about that later on, the Riemann-Hilbert we are dealing with is a non-abelian version of the Flaschka-Newell Lax pair for the second Painlevé equation. The explicit formulas for parametrices are given in the Appendices A-E. We provide comparison with β=2\beta=2 case in Appendix F.

2. Lax pair of the Calogero-Painlevé System

2.1. Matrix Painlevé equation

The following Lax pair considered in [2] is the quantization of Flaschka-Newell pair for the second Painlevé equation

(2.1) d​Wd​z=U⁡(z)​W​(z),d​Wd​t=V⁡(z)​W​(z),\dfrac{dW}{dz}=U(z)W(z),\quad\dfrac{dW}{dt}=V(z)W(z),
U⁡(z)=U2​z2+U1​z+U0+U−1z,V⁡(z)=V1​z+V0,U(z)=U_{2}z^{2}+U_{1}z+U_{0}+\dfrac{U_{-1}}{z},\quad V(z)=V_{1}z+V_{0},
U2=(i​I3200−i​I32),U1=(0qq0),U0=(i​q2+i​t​I32−i​pi​p−i​q2−i​t​I32),U_{2}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\dfrac{\mathrm{i}I_{3}}{2}&0\\ 0&-\dfrac{\mathrm{i}I_{3}}{2}\end{array}\right),\quad U_{1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&q\\ q&0\end{array}\right),\quad U_{0}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathrm{i}q^{2}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}tI_{3}}{2}&-\mathrm{i}p\\ \mathrm{i}p&-\mathrm{i}q^{2}-\dfrac{\mathrm{i}tI_{3}}{2}\end{array}\right),
U−1=(0−θ​I3−θ​I30)U_{-1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&-\theta I_{3}\\ -\theta I_{3}&0\end{array}\right)
V1=U2,V0=U1.V_{1}=U_{2},\quad V_{0}=U_{1}.

Here qq and pp are 3×33\times 3 matrices, compared to standard Flaschka-Newell Lax pair. The compatibility condition takes form of matrix Painlevé II equation

(2.2) d​qd​t=p,d​pd​t=2​q3+t​q+θ​I3.\dfrac{dq}{dt}=p,\quad\dfrac{dp}{dt}=2q^{3}+tq+\theta I_{3}.

The symmetry of the coefficient matrix

−U⁡(−z)=(σ1⊗I3)​U​(z)​(σ1⊗I3).-U(-z)=({\sigma}_{1}\otimes I_{3})U(z)({\sigma}_{1}\otimes I_{3}).

implies the symmetry of solution

(2.3) W⁡(−z)=(σ1⊗I3)​W​(z)​(σ1⊗I3).W(-z)=(\sigma_{1}\otimes I_{3})W(z)(\sigma_{1}\otimes I_{3}).

We have the following asymptotic at infinity

(2.4) W⁡(z)=(I6+n1z+O⁡(1z2))​e(ln⁡z+i​π​ε)​(I2⊗[q,p])​ei2​(z33+t​z)​(σ3⊗I3),W(z)=\left(I_{6}+\dfrac{n_{1}}{z}+O\left(\dfrac{1}{z^{2}}\right)\right)\mathrm{e}^{(\ln z+\mathrm{i}\pi\varepsilon)(I_{2}\otimes[q,p])}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\left(\frac{z^{3}}{3}+tz\right)(\sigma_{3}\otimes I_{3})},

where

ε={0Im⁡(z)≥01Im⁡(z)<0,n^1,12=i​q.\varepsilon=\begin{cases}0&\mathrm{Im}(z)\geq 0\\ 1&\mathrm{Im}(z)<0\\ \end{cases},\quad\hat{n}_{1,12}=\mathrm{i}q.

The asymptotic at the origin has form

(2.5) W(z)=G0(I6+O(z))e(lnz+iπε)(−θσ3⊗I3)(K⊗I3)−1,z→0,W(z)=G_{0}\left(I_{6}+O\left(z\right)\right)\mathrm{e}^{(\ln z+\mathrm{i}\pi\varepsilon){(-\theta\sigma_{3}\otimes I_{3})}}(K\otimes I_{3})^{-1},\quad z\to 0,

with

(2.6) G0=(K⊗I3)​(r100r2),K=I2−i​σ22=12​(1−111),K​σ3=σ1​K,σ3​K=−K​σ1.G_{0}=(K\otimes I_{3})\begin{pmatrix}r_{1}&0\\ 0&r_{2}\\ \end{pmatrix},\quad K=\dfrac{I_{2}-\mathrm{i}\sigma_{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&-1\\ 1&1\end{array}\right),\quad K\sigma_{3}=\sigma_{1}K,\quad\sigma_{3}K=-K\sigma_{1}.

We would like to notice that the choice of g=±i3g=\pm\frac{\mathrm{i}}{3} makes the operator Id+ad[q,p]\mathrm{Id}+\mathrm{ad}_{[q,p]} not invertible and to find m1m_{1} we would need to use standard procedure presented in [12] and not in [2].

d​r1d​t=q​r1,d​r2d​t=−q​r2.\dfrac{dr_{1}}{dt}=qr_{1},\quad\dfrac{dr_{2}}{dt}=-qr_{2}.

2.2. Calogero-Painlevé system of equations

The commutator [p,q][p,q] is preserved by dynamics (2.2), so it is part of monodromy data. We will choose it from Calogero-Moser space

(2.7) [p,q]=i​g​(I3−vT​v)=−i​g​(011101110),v=(1,1,…,1).[p,q]=\mathrm{i}g(I_{3}-v^{T}v)=-\mathrm{i}g\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&1&1\\ 1&0&1\\ 1&1&0\end{array}\right),\quad v=(1,1,\ldots,1).

Below we list the results from [2]. It is possible to conjugate matrices qq and pp in such a way that

q=𝒪​X​𝒪−1,X=(x1000x2000x3),q=\mathcal{O}X\mathcal{O}^{-1},\quad X=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}x_{1}&0&0\\ 0&x_{2}&0\\ 0&0&x_{3}\end{array}\right),
p=𝒪​Y​𝒪−1,Y=(y1i​g(x1−x2)i​g(x1−x3)i​g(x2−x1)y2i​g(x2−x3)i​g(x3−x1)i​g(x3−x2)y3).p=\mathcal{O}Y\mathcal{O}^{-1},\quad Y=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}y_{1}&\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{1}-x_{2})}&\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{1}-x_{3})}\\ \dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{2}-x_{1})}&y_{2}&\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{2}-x_{3})}\\ \dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{3}-x_{1})}&\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{3}-x_{2})}&y_{3}\end{array}\right).

F=(f1−i​g(x1−x2)2−i​g(x1−x3)2−i​g(x2−x1)2f2−i​g(x2−x3)2−i​g(x3−x1)2−i​g(x3−x2)2f3),F=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}f_{1}&-\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}}&-\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{1}-x_{3})^{2}}\\ -\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}}&f_{2}&-\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{2}-x_{3})^{2}}\\ -\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{3}-x_{1})^{2}}&-\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{(x_{3}-x_{2})^{2}}&f_{3}\end{array}\right),
f1=−2​i​g3​1(x2−x3)2+i​g3​1(x1−x3)2+i​g3​1(x2−x1)2,f_{1}=-\dfrac{2\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{2}-x_{3})^{2}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{1}-x_{3})^{2}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}},
f2=−2​i​g3​1(x1−x3)2+i​g3​1(x2−x3)2+i​g3​1(x2−x1)2,f_{2}=-\dfrac{2\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{1}-x_{3})^{2}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{2}-x_{3})^{2}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}},
f3=−2​i​g3​1(x2−x1)2+i​g3​1(x1−x3)2+i​g3​1(x2−x3)2.f_{3}=-\dfrac{2\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{2}-x_{1})^{2}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{1}-x_{3})^{2}}+\dfrac{\mathrm{i}g}{3}\dfrac{1}{(x_{2}-x_{3})^{2}}.

Taking it into account, one can rewrite the compatibility conditions (2.2) as

d​Xd​t=Y+[X,F],d​Yd​t=2​X3+t​X+θ​I3+[Y,F].\dfrac{dX}{dt}=Y+[X,F],\quad\dfrac{dY}{dt}=2X^{3}+tX+\theta I_{3}+[Y,F].

It implies that eigenvalues of matrix qq satisfy Calogero Painlevé system of equations (1.1).

In the case of β=2\beta=2 though there is a way out without using the alternative formula (F.5). In what follows we shall describe how indeed the problem can be solved in the case β=2\beta=2.

We shall need a few general facts from [12] concerning the solutions of the second Painlevé equation (F.1) with the asymptotic behavior (F.3) on the minus infinity.

Proposition F.1 ([12], Theorems 11.2 and 11.3).

Remark F.5.

Strictly speaking Theorems 11.2, 11.3, 11.5, 11.6 are proven in [12] only for α−12∉ℤ\alpha-\frac{1}{2}\notin\mathbb{Z}. The relevant extension can be produced after reasonable effort.

Let us proceed now with showing that formula (F.2) yields the estimate (F.6). We first observe that formulae (F.10) implies that the solution x0​(t)x_{0}(t), in addition to the Painlevé equation (F.1), also satisfies the Riccati equation,

Let’s come back to β=6\beta=6. Keeping in mind the just described β=2\beta=2 case, a natural idea of how to transform estimate (1.50) into estimate (1.31) would be to find a β=6\beta=6 analog of the explicit solution x0​(t)x_{0}(t). In more details, we are thinking of the following program.

First we notice that similar to (F.2), equation (1.30) can be rewritten as,

(F.18) logF6(−2−1/3t)=12∫−∞t(t−s)Tr(q′(s)−q2(s)−s2)ds\log F_{6}(-2^{-1/3}t)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{t}(t-s)\mathrm{Tr}\left(q^{\prime}(s)-q^{2}(s)-\frac{s}{2}\right)ds

where q⁡(t)q(t) is the solution of the matrix Painlevé II equation (2.2) whose eigenvalues, x1​(t)x_{1}(t), x2​(t)x_{2}(t), x3​(t)x_{3}(t) form the solution (1.29), (1.36). Similar to the case β=2\beta=2, our goal is to show that

(F.19) Tr(q′(t)−q2(t)−t2)=121​π2−13/2(−t)−7/2e−2​2​(−t)3/2(1+o(1)),t→−∞.\mathrm{Tr}\left(q^{\prime}(t)-q^{2}(t)-\frac{t}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{21\pi}2^{-13/2}(-t)^{-7/2}\mathrm{e}^{-2\sqrt{2}(-t)^{3/2}}\Bigl(1+o(1)\Bigr),\quad t\rightarrow-\infty.

Indeed, similar (F.17) in the case of β=2\beta=2, this estimate produces, via the integral formula (F.18), the needed estimate (F.6) for the right tail of the Tracy-Widom distribution F6​(t)F_{6}(t).

Using again the experience we have gained in the case β=2\beta=2, a natural way to proceed is to try to find a special, presumably explicit solution (x01​(t),x02​(t),x03​(t))(x_{01}(t),x_{02}(t),x_{03}(t)) of the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29) such that it belongs to the four parameter family (3.3), (3.5). of the solutions and for the corresponding solution q0​(t)q_{0}(t) of the matrix Painlevé II equation (2.2) a matrix analog of the Riccati equation (F.15),

(F.20) Tr⁡(q0′​(t)−q02​(t)−t2)=0\mathrm{Tr}\left(q^{\prime}_{0}(t)-q^{2}_{0}(t)-\frac{t}{2}\right)=0

holds. If, in addition, we will be able to show that for a proper constant matrix CC, the matrix Painlevé II function q⁡(t)q(t) corresponding to the solution (3.6) of the Calogero-Painlevé system (1.29) satisfies the asymptotic relation (cf. (F.11)),

(F.21) q⁡(t)−q0​(t)=C​1(−t)9/2​e−2​2​(−t)3/2​(1+o⁡(1)),q(t)-q_{0}(t)=C\frac{1}{(-t)^{9/2}}\mathrm{e}^{-2\sqrt{2}(-t)^{3/2}}\Bigl(1+o(1)\Bigr),
|t|→∞,arg⁡t=π+arg⁡(−t)∈(2​π3,4​π3),|t|\rightarrow\infty,\quad\arg t=\pi+\arg(-t)\in\left(\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3}\right),

then, again similar to β=2\beta=2 case, we will reach our goal - estimate (F.19). We hope to be able to realize this program in the forthcoming publication.
